proposals.relationship: McKay challenges the extension of Valverde’s Toronto–Ottawa evidence into an undifferentiated English Canada while praising her methodological innovation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 92–93 and note 3, names The Age of Light, Soap and Water and questions its spatial scale, regional typicality and use of a part to stand for a whole. He calls the book pioneering and deserving of praise for its methodology, while suggesting that a Boston–Halifax axis might be more pertinent for some Atlantic questions. This is a specific geographical and historiographical objection, not rejection of moral regulation or a new reading of Valverde’s complete book. The article lightly edits an unpresented 1997 talk and is dated by its 2000 publication; Valverde’s earlier work is not treated as responding to McKay’s later framework.
primary_locators: A Note on Region (2000):92–93/n3; original byline and talk qualification89/n1

proposals.relationship: McKay argues that Cook’s deconstruction of regionalism leaves the category Canada insufficiently questioned.
proposals.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 93/note 4, explicitly identifies Cook’s Regionalism Unmasked (1983) and states this precise objection. The surrounding argument92–94 calls for scrutiny of national categories and scale as well as regional ones. This criticism coexists with Cook’s separate positive use of McKay’s wartime Atlantic history in edge_2692; it is not a blanket verdict on Cook’s career or a freshly audited reading of his 1983 article. The distinct later comment94–95/n7 on the joint Cook/R. Craig Brown national synthesis retains joint authorship and is not needed to infer the narrow new objection.
primary_locators: A Note on Region (2000):93/n4, context92–94; distinct joint synthesis comment94–95/n7

proposals.relationship: McKay explicitly borrows Perry’s frame of Canada at the edges of empires when explaining its combined colonial and colonizing position.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2021 Breach interview, answer on Canada as colonizer and colony, names Adele Perry when borrowing this frame before developing his account of British and United States imperial constraints. This is a bounded conceptual resource in his retrospective explanation, not evidence that Perry originated every part of his liberal-order framework or caused the 2000 prospectus. He neither identifies an exact Perry title here nor claims a personal teaching relationship. Perry’s original books remain unread; McKay’s broad historical and political conclusions remain his own, rather than independent findings of this dossier.
primary_locators: Lukacs interview (2021), colonizer/colony answer, paragraph beginning On the other hand, Canada is set apart; saved web lines91–99
